blocks.text: Practice long questions for the whole of Chapter 5 (Enzymes), in the shape of a Board long question: each theory question carries 4 marks (describe, explain, compare, label and describe a structure, give examples), as one 4-mark part or in 1+3 / 2+2 sub-parts. Each question has a full model answer.

blocks.prompt: 1 Enzymes control the chemistry of life. (i) Explain why enzymes are essential for life. (ii) Describe where enzymes are made and where they work in and out of the cell. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
(i) Metabolism, the sum of all chemical activities of living organisms, is regulated by enzymes. Enzymes are specific proteins (biocatalysts) that speed up specific reactions by lowering the activation energy and are unaltered themselves. Enzyme-catalysed reactions may be 10³ to 10⁸ times faster than uncatalysed ones; a reaction completed in 30 minutes with an enzyme would take one year without it. So without enzymes there would be no life. Different cells (e.g. red blood cells and nerve cells) have different sets of enzymes, so their reactions differ.

(ii) All enzymes are synthesized inside cells by ribosomes. After synthesis they either stay and work inside the cell or are secreted out to work at other sites. Inside the cell:
1. Many are dissolved in the cytoplasm, e.g. enzymes of glycolysis.
2. Many are tightly bound to membranes of certain organelles.
3. Some are an integral part of ribosomes, e.g. enzymes of protein synthesis.

book_ref.quote: Enzymes may be defined as specific proteins that speed up specific chemical reactions

blocks.prompt: 2 Enzymes are highly specific and sometimes dangerous to their own cells. (i) Explain why only a certain substrate fits an active site and how the two regions of the active site act. (ii) Explain why pepsin is secreted as pepsinogen. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
(i) Enzymes are three-dimensional globular proteins of coiled polypeptide chains. A small cleft of only a few amino acids on the surface is the active site, where catalysis occurs. Its shape is very specific, three-dimensional and it bears a specific charge, so only a certain substrate molecule can fit into it. It has two regions:
1. Binding site: the substrate fits into it by weak chemical forces such as hydrogen bonds.
2. Catalytic site: catalyses the reaction, and the substrate is transformed into products.

(ii) Some enzymes may be harmful if active at the wrong place. Pepsin is a protein-digesting enzyme that could destroy protein-made structures inside the cells where it is synthesized. So it is produced in an inactive form, pepsinogen, and secreted out of the cells. When it reaches its target site of action, it is activated to pepsin.

book_ref.quote: When it reaches its target site of action, it is activated (pepsin)

blocks.prompt: 3 Many enzymes need non-protein helpers. (i) Define cofactor, apoenzyme and holoenzyme. (ii) Explain how metal ions work as cofactors, with examples. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
(i) Cofactors are additional non-protein chemical components that many enzymes use to aid catalysis; they are of three kinds: metal ions, prosthetic groups and coenzymes. The protein part of the enzyme is the apoenzyme; the complete enzyme including its cofactor is the holoenzyme (apoenzyme + cofactor = holoenzyme).

(ii) Many enzymes use metal ions such as Ca⁺², Mg⁺², Mn⁺², Cu⁺² and Zn⁺² as cofactors. These metal ions change the non-functional active sites of enzymes into functional sites. The attachment of the cofactor also changes the shape of the enzyme and allows it to combine with the substrate. Trace elements such as molybdenum and manganese, necessary for health, are also used by enzymes as cofactors.

book_ref.quote: Many enzymes use additional chemical components to aid in catalysis

blocks.prompt: 4 Define coenzyme. Explain how coenzymes such as NAD⁺ carry electrons and energy in the cell, and name vitamins that act as coenzymes. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Coenzyme: a cofactor that is a non-protein organic molecule loosely attached with the enzyme.

Role: coenzymes participate in enzyme-catalysed reactions, often by transporting electrons (hydrogen atoms) from one enzyme to another.

NAD⁺: the most important coenzyme in the cell is the hydrogen acceptor nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD⁺). When NAD⁺ acquires a hydrogen atom, it is reduced to NADH. The electron of the hydrogen atom contains energy, which the NADH molecule carries. For example, when food is oxidized in the cell, enzymes draw electrons from food molecules and transfer them to NAD⁺, which is reduced to NADH.

Vitamins: many vitamins, e.g. niacin and riboflavin, function as coenzymes; some are parts of coenzymes.

book_ref.quote: The most important coenzyme in cell is the hydrogen acceptor nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide

blocks.prompt: 5 Describe the steps by which an enzyme converts its substrate into products, and explain how many enzymes work together in a metabolic pathway. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Steps of enzyme action:
1. Due to its specificity, the enzyme recognizes a specific substrate, which binds with the active site.
2. An enzyme-substrate (ES) complex is formed and the catalytic site is activated.
3. The atoms of the catalytic site stress and destabilize particular bonds of the substrate, so the activation energy is lowered.
4. The reaction starts and the substrate is transformed into products.
5. The enzyme detaches from the products in an unaltered state.
Summary: E + S → ES → E + P. The enzyme does not change the nature of products (sucrose always gives glucose and fructose, with or without sucrase).

Enzymes in a pathway: in complex pathways such as respiration, photosynthesis and protein synthesis, many enzymes act in a sequence and regulate the steps. The successive enzymes are present together with their cofactors. The product of one enzyme's catalysis serves as the substrate for the next enzyme. Finally end products are formed, which inhibit the first enzyme through feedback.

book_ref.quote: Due to its specificity, an enzyme recognizes a specific substrate

blocks.prompt: 6 What is denaturation of an enzyme? Explain how very high temperature and extreme pH each bring it about. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Denaturation: the loss of the globular structure of an enzyme, when the bonds can no longer hold the polypeptide chains in their proper position. It causes a rapid decrease in the rate of enzyme action, which may be blocked completely.

By high temperature: the shape of the enzyme protein is held by hydrogen bonds and hydrophobic interactions, which are easily disrupted by temperature changes. When temperature is raised well above the optimum (37 °C for human enzymes), heat increases the vibrations of the atoms of the enzyme. When vibrations become too violent, the bonds cannot hold the polypeptide chains in position and the globular structure is lost. (Thermophilic bacteria resist this because their proteins have stronger bonding; they work at 70 °C or more.)

By extreme pH: in the globular structure, chains are also held by bonds between oppositely charged amino acids such as glutamic acid (–) and lysine (+). These bonds are sensitive to hydrogen ion concentration. A pH change alters the ionization of active-site amino acids (and of the substrate); an extreme change breaks these bonds, resulting in denaturation.

book_ref.quote: The shape of a protein is determined by the hydrogen bonds and hydrophobic interactions

blocks.prompt: 7 Explain the effect of pH on the rate of enzyme action, with examples of enzymes and their optimum pH. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
1. All enzymes work at their maximum rate at a narrow range of pH; a slight increase or decrease retards enzyme activity or blocks it completely.
2. Each enzyme works best at a specific pH, its optimum pH. Pepsin is active in acidic medium (low pH); trypsin shows optimum activity in alkaline medium (high pH). Papain from green papaya works in both acidic and alkaline media.
3. Reason: polypeptide chains are held by bonds between oppositely charged amino acids (glutamic acid – and lysine +), which are sensitive to H⁺ concentration. A pH change can change the ionization of active-site amino acids and of the substrate. Extreme pH breaks these bonds and denatures the enzyme.

Optimum pH of some human enzymes:

book_ref.quote: All enzymes work at their maximum rate at a narrow range of pH

blocks.prompt: 8 Compare the effect of increasing enzyme concentration with that of increasing substrate concentration on the rate of enzyme action. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: Both raise the rate at first and then the rate levels off, but for different reasons:

book_ref.quote: If enzyme concentration is kept constant and the amount of substrate is increased

rows: Substrate concentration unlimited (or kept the same later)
Rate depends directly on the amount of enzyme present
Rate increases while enzymes have vacant active sites
More enzyme molecules give more active sites, so more substrate is bound and transformed
New substrate binds the free active sites, so more product forms in the given time
If substrate stays the same, no more substrate attaches to extra enzyme
At high substrate all active sites are occupied; extra substrate finds no free site
Rate stays constant and does not increase further
A point is reached where more substrate does not increase the rate

blocks.prompt: 9 Explain reversible and irreversible inhibition of enzymes with examples. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Whether an inhibitor acts reversibly or irreversibly depends on the kind of bond formed between inhibitor and enzyme.

Irreversible inhibitors: make covalent bonds with the enzyme. They cannot be released by dilution or dialysis or by increasing the substrate concentration. Examples: penicillin permanently disables the enzyme responsible for building bacterial cell walls; the poison cyanide combines with copper and iron in the active site of cytochrome oxidase and blocks cellular respiration.

Reversible inhibitors: make weak bonds (e.g. hydrogen bonds) with the enzyme. They can be released, and their inhibition can be neutralized by increasing the substrate concentration. Example: malonate temporarily slows the reaction by blocking succinate dehydrogenase, an enzyme of cellular respiration; the inhibition is reversed when malonate is removed.

book_ref.quote: Such inhibitors cannot be released by dilution or dialysis or by increasing the concentration of substrate

blocks.prompt: 10 Enzyme inhibitors can heal or kill. (i) Explain how inhibitors are used as drugs, with examples. (ii) Explain how some inhibitors act as poisons, and how competitive antibiotics kill bacteria. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
(i) As drugs:
1. Aspirin inhibits the enzymes that produce prostaglandin (which causes inflammation), so it suppresses pain and inflammation.
2. Antibiotics inhibit the enzymes of bacteria; cancer drugs may inhibit enzymes involved in cell division.
3. Inhibitors of enzymes involved in blood clotting are used as anticoagulants.
4. Inhibitors are tools in pharmaceutical research to study enzyme function and potential drugs.

(ii) As poisons: some toxins and poisons inhibit important enzymes in the body; e.g. cyanide is an irreversible inhibitor that combines with copper and iron in the active site of cytochrome oxidase and blocks cellular respiration. Understanding such inhibition helps in treating poisoning.
Competitive antibiotics: their molecules are similar in structure to the substrates of bacterial enzymes necessary for the bacteria's life (book correction: substrates, not enzymes). They bind to and block the active sites of those enzymes, so the bacteria are killed.

book_ref.quote: Inhibitors are often used as drugs, but they can also act as poisons

blocks.prompt: 11 The end product of a pathway can regulate its own production. (i) Explain how the final product shuts down a metabolic pathway, with the ATP example. (ii) Explain how succinyl-CoA controls its own formation. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
(i) In a metabolic pathway the product of one reaction is the substrate of the next, and at the end a desired product is made. To regulate its concentration the pathway must be shut down. The final product acts as an inhibitor: it reacts with an initial enzyme and changes its conformation, so that enzyme can no longer bind its substrate; the pathway closes and no more product is made. Example: when a cell has more ATP than it needs, ATP itself acts as a non-competitive inhibitor and blocks the enzyme that catalyses ATP synthesis.

(ii) Succinic acid and CoA react to form succinyl-CoA, catalysed by succinyl-CoA synthetase. After its formation, succinyl-CoA acts as a non-competitive inhibitor and binds with the enzyme; the enzyme is inhibited and no more succinyl-CoA is produced.

book_ref.quote: That enzyme can no longer bind to its substrate

blocks.prompt: 12 Using the classification of enzymes by substrate, describe how proteins, carbohydrates and lipids are broken down by enzymes. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Proteins (proteases):
1. Pepsin and trypsin break large polypeptides into smaller polypeptides.
2. Erepsin breaks dipeptides into amino acids (book correction: printed 'erypsin').

Carbohydrates (carbohydrases): they break bigger carbohydrates into smaller units.
1. Amylase breaks starch or glycogen into maltose; maltase breaks maltose into glucose.
2. Sucrase breaks sucrose into glucose and fructose; lactase breaks lactose into glucose and galactose.
3. Cellulase breaks cellulose into cellobiose (a disaccharide) or glucose.

Lipids (lipases): pancreatic lipase hydrolyses lipids into fatty acids and glycerol.

(Nucleic acids are broken down by nucleases such as RNAase and DNAase.)

book_ref.quote: pepsin and trypsin enzymes catalyse the breakdown of large polypeptides

blocks.prompt: 13 Enzymes are grouped by the type of reaction they catalyse. (i) Differentiate between transferases and lyases. (ii) Differentiate between oxidoreductases and isomerases. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
(i) Transferases: catalyse the transfer of a specific functional group (e.g. methyl, acyl, amino or phosphate) from one substrate to another; e.g. hexokinase transfers a phosphate group from ATP to glucose.
Lyases: catalyse the non-hydrolytic addition or removal of groups (e.g. CO₂, NH₂) from substrates; e.g. pyruvate decarboxylase removes CO₂ from pyruvic acid.

(ii) Oxidoreductases: catalyse oxidation/reduction of substrates by adding or removing H⁺ ions or electrons; e.g. cytochrome oxidase catalyses the oxidation of cytochrome.
Isomerases: catalyse intra-molecular rearrangement, converting one isomer into another; e.g. hexose isomerase converts glucose to fructose.

book_ref.quote: The enzymes of this class catalyse the transfer of a specific functional group
